title: Equality at home
hook: sharing work fairly between women and men
tomorrow: Arjan's family is new and still unpacking. what do you bring?

segments.voice: Yesterday, no caste: one light, and Guru Gobind Singh's whole human race as one. Bebe is still thinking. Today the same question walks into the kitchen.

Sunday lunch at Simran's house. Her aunts are at the stove, rolling, frying, plating. Her uncles are on the couch with the match on, calling for more chai. Nobody planned it. It's just how the room arranges itself, every time. Simran carries out a tray, sets it down, and says, loud enough to hear over the TV: in the langar, everybody cooks. The room goes quiet. Then her dad, Harjit, gets up, a little awkward, and picks up a dish towel.
screen: `AUNTS AT THE STOVE.` → `UNCLES ON THE COUCH.` → `IN THE LANGAR, EVERYBODY COOKS.` → `HARJIT PICKS UP A TOWEL.`

segments.voice: Simran wasn't inventing a rule. In Asa di Var, on Ang 473, Guru Nanak looks at how people talked about women and turns it around. In paraphrase: we are born of woman, we're shaped in woman, we marry woman, and when one woman is gone we seek another. So why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? And in the langar, the free kitchen, the work isn't sorted by who you are: anyone can knead dough, stir the pot, serve, or wash up. Today's word is that same kitchen, brought home. Now look back over the week, because every day of it stood in this kitchen too. Stand up: Simran named the wrong out loud, peacefully first. Dignity: say who you are, plainly. Without fear, which isn't the same as without shaking. Wait with the name, a bead at a time. Accept, then rise, after half a win. And no caste: one light in everyone. Equal at home is all six, on a Sunday. Bebe, watching her son dry a plate, laughs so hard she has to sit down.
screen: `WHY CALL HER LESSER?` · `IN THE LANGAR, ANYONE COOKS.` · `SIX DAYS IN ONE KITCHEN.` · `EQUAL AT HOME IS ALL SIX.` · then, large: `EQUAL AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the people whose unseen work kept your home running this week: who cooked, who cleaned, who remembered, who drove. Say each name quietly and what they did. When you run out of fingers, notice whose name came up most, and whether you'd ever thanked them.
Equality at home. Sharing the work fairly between women and men, the way the langar shares it.
For the week ahead: equal at home, a dish towel in everyone's hands. Seven days, one kitchen, and Bebe still laughing.

screen: `DAY 1729 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 103 OF 134.` → `TOMORROW: ARJAN'S FAMILY IS STILL UNPACKING. WHAT DO YOU BRING?`

howItsDone: In the gurdwara langar, women and men cook, serve and wash up side by side, and some Sikh families talk about bringing that same sharing of work home.

chat.says: dad dried every dish. my uncles are acting like i started a war. was i out of line?
options: not out of line. Guru Nanak asked why call her lesser; you asked kindly.
a bit. the langar is for the gurdwara; home can run its own way.
yes. you only speak up at home if an elder asks you first.
chat.meaning: Guru Nanak asks why woman is called lesser, and in the langar anyone cooks. Saying it kindly at home is standing up, peacefully first.
